title: The Beefeater Defense
description: A tricky system against d4, c4, and Nc3, which tries to take your opponents out of their comfort zone into murky positions.

r1b1k1nr/p2p1p1p/2p3p1/q3p3/2P1P3/2P1Q3/.text: Most natural retreat, keeping defense on c3.

r1b1k1nr/p2ppp1p/2p3p1/q7/2PQP3/2P5/P4PP.text:
Hitting the rook and defending c3.

We can block with a tempo.

r1b1k1nr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/q7/2P5/2P5/P1NBP.text: As we see several times, the bishop does not scare us in the least.

r1b1k1nr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/q1n5/2P5/2P3P1/P2B.text: Black has great influence in the center, and should be extremely comfortable.

r1b1k1nr/pp1ppp1p/n5p1/q1P5/2P5/2P3P1/P2.text: This might be a way for White to develop.

r1b1k2r/3ppp1p/1pn2np1/q7/2P5/2P1QN2/P3P.text:
Black's pieces are on great squares, with clear targets to attack.

The a-file is semi-open and we will develop the bishop to a6 with even more pressure.

r1b1k2r/p2p1p1p/2p2np1/q3p3/2P1P3/2P1Q3/.text:
Black has a variety of plans they can go for.

They consist of playing against the weak c-pawns, blasting the position open with ...d5, or activating the bishop on the active a6-f1 diagonal.

We'll castle short.

r1b1k2r/p2ppp1p/1Pn2np1/q7/2P5/2P1QN2/P3.text: Natural. If White doesn't take, Black will happily take on c5.

r1b1k2r/p3ppbp/6p1/3p4/8/4P3/PP2BPPP/R1B.text:
And we recapture with our d-pawn.

It could even be said we stand slightly better out of the opening because our g7-bishop is very strong.

We will also have great play on the a- and b-files.

r1b1k2r/pp1ppp1p/2n2np1/q1P3B1/2P5/2P1Q3.text: And when it retreats, we can attack it yet again.

r1b1k2r/pp1ppp1p/2n2np1/q1P5/2P1P3/2P1Q3.text:
The move Qe3 defends c3 and e4.

However, the queen is overloaded, so it won't last...

r1b1k2r/pp1ppp1p/2n2np1/q1P5/2P5/2P1QN2/.text:
Moving the queen away while simultaneously defending the c3-pawn.

White is very passive. Let's continue in a gambit style.

r1b1k2r/pp1ppp1p/2n2np1/q7/2P5/2P5/P1NBP.text:
Black has ideas to attack the doubled pawns, which is what makes this position good.

We'll play ...b6 to activate the bishop to a6 and add pressure to the c4-pawn.

Castling short is natural.

r1b1k2r/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/2P5/2P1Q3/2q5/P4P.text:
Netting an exchange, and Black is completely winning.

White shouldn't play like this.

r1b1k2r/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/2q3B1/2P3n1/2P5/P.text:
And we can take on c5, putting pressure on f2 and on the bishop.

c4 is also hit, and ...d6 and ...Be6 is a good plan.

Black is much better here.

r1b1k2r/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/q1P5/2P1Q3/2P5/P4.text: White can decline the sacrifice, but this is obviously the critical variation.

r1bqk1nr/p2ppp1p/2p3p1/8/2P1P3/2P5/P4PPP.text:
Only move.

Our queen comes out and attacks c3.

This is a very common motif we will go over in many variations White plays.

The whole point of giving away our dark-squared bishop is to go after White's weak pawns.

r1bqk1nr/p2pppbp/2p3p1/8/2P1P3/2N5/PP3PP.text:
Taking control of the center seems very logical.

Let's wreck the pawn structure.

r1bqk1nr/pp1ppp1p/2n3p1/8/2P5/2P5/P1N1PP.text:
Only move.

We now attack c3.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2N3p1/8/2P5/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
Also a critical move, simply capturing the knight.

We recapture.

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/8/2P5/2N5/PPN1PP.text:
If White is "smart", they'll try to maintain the tension and keep both knights on the board.

But we can take one!

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/8/2PN4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
e3 is a very popular move, supporting the knight.

We develop the kingside in a natural manner.

r1bqk2r/p3ppbp/2p3p1/3N4/8/4P3/PP2BPPP/R.text:
White goes for massive trades.

We don't mind.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/8/2PN4/2N1P3/PP2.text:
White continues with development.

Let's strike in the center.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2N3p1/3n4/8/2N1P3/PP2BPP.text:
They take on c6.

We can recapture and support our knight.

r1bqk2r/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/3P4/3N4/2N1P3/PP2.text:
White takes.

We'll recapture and activate our minor pieces.

rn1qk1nr/pp3p1p/3pb1p1/2p5/2P5/2P1P3/P4P.text: Black has a d5-break to go for, and overall fluid development.

rnb1k1nr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/q1P5/2P5/2P5/P2BPP.text:
Not a scary attempt, as White would need to move three pawns in order for the bishop to contact the queen. 

...Na6 is great to involve another piece.

We'll also activate the kingside knight to f6 and look to push either ...b6 or ...d6 to activate the light-squared bishop once we capture on c5.

rnb1k1nr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/q1P5/2PQ4/2P5/P3PP.text:
This is the move that White will play if they are smart. 

Defending both pawns while attacking our rook.

We develop and block.

rnb1k2r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/q1P3B1/2PQ4/2P5/P3.text:
This is a very popular blunder, attacking the knight.

We can develop with a tempo and attack the queen, which defends c3.

rnb1k2r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/q1P5/2PQ4/2P2N2/P3.text:
White doesn't have any scary options, so they may continue development as normal.

Let's get developed with a tempo.

rnb1k2r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/q1P5/2PQP3/2P5/P4P.text:
A slightly more aggressive "developing" attempt is e4, activating the bishop.

We'll force the queen away.

rnbQk1nr/pp2pp1p/6p1/2p5/2P5/2P1P3/P4PPP.text: White doesn't have to trade Queens, but it's probably the most logical

rnbk2nr/pp2pp1p/6p1/2p5/2P5/2P1P3/P4PPP/.text: This "Queen trade" position is not as bad as it may appear...

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White does the same.

And now d5 is a good move.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2Pp4/3P4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
After c5, we should be fine after Ne4.

We have strong central play with the knight on e4, which is tricky for White to take because of tactics on the d4-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2P5/2P5/2P5/P3PPPP.text:
Look at that structure!

Our queen can come out and target two of the pawns.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2P5/2P5/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
Our first point of investigation will be what if White just takes the pawn? 

Free pawn, right? It's not exactly like that.

Let's take the knight!

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p5/2PP4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
A tame attempt by White to defend the center, and minimize any damages done in the center.

We'll maintain the tension, and if White touches their d-pawn to move it, we'll chop the c3-Knight off beefeater style.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2p5/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
You'll very likely see this "solid" approach by White, not wanting to engage with conflict in the center.

Let's capture on d4 in that case.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/8/2PN4/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
White recaptures.

Let's develop and create more tension in the center.

rnbqk1nr/pp2pp1p/3p2p1/2P5/2P5/2P1P3/P4P.text:
Only recapture.

In this instance, we actually want to allow the Queen trade. The natural Qa5 runs into a slippery slope after cxd6! Qxc3, Bd2, and Black is in trouble.

rnbqk1nr/pp2pp1p/3p2p1/2pP4/2P5/2P1P3/P4.text:
Only move.

Now we push ...e5. An interesting stockfish suggestion... It's by no means necessary, but if White allows it, you can go f5 and put your pawns in motion.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/3p2p1/2P5/2P5/2N1P3/PP3.text: This capture is always something to consider, but we take on c3.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/3p2p1/2p5/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
White just develops their knight.

And so we continue developing as well.

rnbqk1nr/pp2ppbp/3p2p1/2pP4/2P5/2N1P3/PP.text:
Honestly, not sure why White would refrain from pushing d5 only to do it the next move... but it's always a consideration.

We take on c3.

rnbqk1nr/pp3p1p/3pP1p1/2p5/2P5/2P1P3/P4P.text: White will probably follow the unwritten "if I can go en passant, I must go en passant."

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
This is a standard approach by White, eyeing more central squares, and in many cases, Nc3 defends e4.

Black can now challenge the center.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2p5/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text: Suppose white just develops, we simply take on the center.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2B.text:
White recaptures.

We get our king to safety.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White puts a second pawn in the center. 

Let's get the bishop fianchettoed.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
This course covers the Beefeater opening. 

After our confrontational 3... c5, the main line is for White to play 4. d5, however, this study will cover the sidelines (taking on c5, and protecting the pawn). 

It's also important to know these lines. Have fun eating beef, unless you're vegetarian!

rnb1k1nr/pp2p2p/3p2p1/q1pP1pB1/2P5/2P5/P.text:
We'll continue our development scheme, and play a solid position.

Our knights are coming to f6 and d7 and our dark-squared pawn chain nicely compensates for the absence of our bishop.

rnb1k2r/pp2p2p/3p1npB/q1pP1p2/2P5/2P2N2/.text:
We'll continue to play on the dark squares.

...Ng4 will likely kick the bishop away, and Black is doing fine.

If White insists with h3, we have ideas such as ...Ne4 or even ...Nd7/...Ne5/...Nf7 to attack the bishop in some positions.

We should eventually be able to castle short.

rnbqk1nr/pp1p3p/4P1p1/2p2p2/2P5/2P5/P1Q1.text:
En passant is always something to consider.

We'll recapture.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pp2p/6p1/2pP1p2/2P5/2P2N2/P3.text:
Nf3 is a good way for White to develop calmly.

Let's answer similarly.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pp2p/6p1/2pP1p2/2P5/2P5/P1Q1.text:
A logical move to try to prepare for a central expansion.

We can strike in the center now, grabbing as much space as possible!

rnbqk1nr/pp1pp2p/6p1/2pP1pB1/2P5/2P5/P3P.text:
Bg5 might come as an inconvenience to pin the e5-pawn.

White is threatening d6.

Which is why we will move the queen out of the way and attack the c3-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2pP4/2P5/2P5/P3PPP.text:
White recaptures, damaging their pawn structure.

And now I recommend ...f5 to control the e4-square and give us more space in the center and on the kingside.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2pP4/2P5/2N5/PP2PP.text:
Advancing the pawn is very logical for White.

However, it opens up our "Beefeater" opportunity.

We'll take the knight!

rnbqk1nr/pp5p/4p1p1/2p2p2/2P4P/2P5/P1Q1P.text:
White may try to belligerently attack the kingside.

However, it won't faze us.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
This is a standard approach by White, eyeing more central squares, and in many cases, Nc3 defends e4.

We'll strike in the center with ...c5.

rnbqk2r/pp1pp2p/5npB/2pP1p2/2P5/2P2N2/P3.text:
Bh6 prevents castling. However, it won't affect us long-term.

Let's go for the usual ...Qa5 and attack the weak c3-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp5p/4pnp1/2p2p2/2P4P/2P5/P1Q1PP.text:
Black has a solid position.

We will bravely castle kingside and look to improve with ...Nc6 and ...e5 if White allows it.

If White plays Bg5 to pin your knight, don't be afraid to play ...h6.

In Chapter 3, we will look at h5 motifs in more detail.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White puts a second pawn in the center. 

Let's fianchetto the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the second study of our Beefeater! 

For this study and next study in the next chapter, we will analyze the main line with 4. d5, starting with "solid" responses for White.

r1b1k1r1/pp1np3/3p1np1/q1pP1pB1/2P5/2P1P.text:
White plays a rational developing move.

Let's rotate the d7-knight to the queenside, from where it puts pressure on c4.

r1b1k1r1/pp2p3/1n1p1np1/q1pP1pB1/2P5/2P1.text:
White continues with simple development.

Our pieces can find useful squares on the queenside.

r1bqk1nr/pp1P3p/2n3p1/2p5/2P1p3/2P2P2/P5.text:
White continues by grabbing another pawn, which is fine.

We'll just recapture with the bishop.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p3p/2n1P1p1/2p5/2P1p3/2P1BP2.text:
White attacks c5.

In that case, we will just defend it with ...d6.

The e6-pawn isn't going anywhere.

r1bqk1nr/pp5p/2npP1p1/2p5/2P1p3/2P1BP2/P.text:
White develops. 

The pawn is ours to take now.

r2qk1nr/pp1b3p/2nQ2p1/2p5/2P1p3/2P2P2/P5.text:
Qd6 is suggested by the engine.

In that case, we will offer a trade on f6 to try and activate our knight.

r2qk1nr/pp5p/2npb1p1/2p5/2P1p3/2P1BP2/P2.text:
You'll notice White's development is hindered by the move f3 as the knight would've loved to go there.

For the near future, ...Qh4+ could be an immediate idea to further worsen White's pawn structure.

Apart from that, we will develop the knight to f6 and castle.

r3k1r1/pp1bp3/1n1p1np1/q1pP1pB1/2P5/2P1P.text:
Suppose White does find this idea, to defend the queenside against our pieces.

We can still improve the bishop to a4 and pressure White's queen.

r3k1r1/pp2p3/1n1p1np1/q1pP1pB1/b1P5/1NP1.text:
If White neglects the e4-square, we can make use of it by trading.

So let's take the knight.

r3k1r1/pp2p3/1n1p2p1/q1pP1pB1/2P1n3/1QP1.text:
And now we fork the pawn and the bishop and Black is much better if not winning.

In the end, White's advances haven't paid off and we ended up being the side that's attacking anyway.

r4rk1/pp1b3p/2n2np1/2p3B1/2P1p3/2P2P2/P5.text:
But we connect rooks, and stand fully developed.

Black is better here because White hasn't dealt with the central tension.

We will look to take on f3 if White doesn't take on e4 now.

rnb1k1nr/pp1p3p/6p1/2pPp3/2P1P2q/2P5/P2K.text: White avoids losing the pawn with check.

rnb1k1nr/pp1p3p/6p1/2pPp3/2P1q3/2P5/P2K2.text:
But the pawn is ours either way.

From a human standpoint, I would argue this position is better for Black.

rnb1k1r1/pp1pp3/5np1/q1pP1p2/2P5/2P2N2/P.text:
White defends naturally.

Let's connect the pawns.

rnb1k1r1/pp2p3/3p1np1/q1pP1pB1/2P5/2P2N2.text:
Now it makes sense to develop the bishop. 

White is threatening to worsen our structure, but we aren't afraid of that. 

We will support the knight on f6 with the knight on d7 for now, but we actually have other plans.

rnbqk1nr/pp1p3p/4P1p1/2p5/2P1p3/2P2P2/P5.text:
En passant is often played. This isn't losing for White.

We can just proceed dynamically by developing our knight.

We don't need to recapture and let White trade the queens.

rnbqk1nr/pp1p3p/6p1/2pPp3/2P1P3/2P5/P5PP.text:
This move has been played many times.

It allows us to give a check on h4.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pp2p/6p1/2pP1p2/2P1P3/2P5/P4.text:
However, what if White plays e4 anyway?

First of all, no reason not to trade on e4.

We played ...f5 with the intention of disallowing White to keep a pawn on e4.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pp2p/6p1/2pP1p2/2P4P/2P5/P3P.text:
White may once again try to storm us on the kingside.

Let's develop the knight and await their response.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pp2p/6p1/2pP4/2P1p3/2P2P2/P5.text:
White potentially gives up any hopes of winning the pawn back, and strives for rapid development.

We won't bite and let them get the knight out.

Let's advance in the center instead.

rnbqk1nr/pp1ppp1p/6p1/2pP4/2P5/2P5/P3PPP.text:
White recaptures, damaging their pawn structure.

Let's gain some space in the center.

rnbqk1nr/pp1pppbp/6p1/2pP4/2P5/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White plays d5.

Let's take the knight.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
This is a standard approach by White.

We can immediately initiate contact in the center.

rnbqk1r1/pp1pp2p/5nP1/2pP1p2/2P5/2P5/P3P.text:
White could leave the pawn sitting there, but we'll assume a capture ensues.

We'll recapture with the pawn, naturally.

rnbqk1r1/pp1pp3/5np1/2pP1p2/2P5/2P2N2/P3.text:
White develops normally.

Since there is no immediate aggression by them, it's time to make some improving moves of our own.

We'll start with attacking the c3-pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp1pp2p/5np1/2pP1p1P/2P5/2P5/P3P.text:
White continues to push the pawn forward, in hopes of damaging our pawn structure.

Capturing the pawn on h5 might be fine but there is no need to give White the h-file.

We can answer with a safe but logical move, which is sliding to the g-file and defending everything.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White puts a second pawn in the center.

Let's place our bishop on g7.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to our third and final study of the Beefeater. 

This chapter will be important when you face experienced and aggressive players. 

This chapter focuses on the direct and aggressive lines against the Beefeater. Study up!
